history: 5da382fd59222819cff110f85ca738a74fb335d1 feat(skills): require explicit merge modes (#10978)

notes: Lines 1-250 show a 6,179-line portability service directly coupled to database tables, shared DTOs, adapter-utils, an OpenCode-local adapter, server adapter registry, GitHub fetch, storage, secrets, org-chart rendering and most domain services. Portability is not a narrow application boundary; vendor/runtime/presentation concerns all flow inward.

The bundle writes schema version 6 and treats unstamped bundles as version 5. Inline completeness relies on an optional client-declared expectedFileCount and rejects only received<expected; it does not authenticate the set, reject extra files or replace a manifest-level canonical file inventory/digest.

Agent-safe mode is implemented as a blacklist of selected project workspace commands/settings and non-schedule triggers. This is vulnerable to policy drift as new executable fields/capabilities are added; Company OS needs capability/data classifications with default-deny admission.

Org-tree export hardcodes English role labels and active status in the service, silently treats missing-parent Agents as roots, omits pure reporting cycles, and leaves an unused rootSlugs set. Presentation and validation are mixed into migration logic.

Lines 251-500 devote substantial portability logic to Paperclip skill identity/provenance and export directory naming across catalog, GitHub, skills.sh, URL, bundled and local-path sources. This is product/vendor-specific taxonomy rather than a neutral migration kernel.

Skill paths are ASCII-normalized, lowercased by default and collision-resolved deterministically with source suffixes then truncated eight-hex hashes. The behavior is useful for stable exports but may collapse international names/case-sensitive identities; original canonical key/source provenance must remain authoritative and collision mapping must be explicit in a manifest.

Lines 501-750 redact secret_ref values and heuristic-sensitive plain env defaults, omit PATH, and label absolute-command defaults system-dependent. The key-name heuristic is neither a data classification contract nor complete secret detection (for example generic key/DSN/cert material can evade it, while unrelated names containing auth can be over-redacted).

Portable env inputs are always marked optional and generated descriptions are English. Original binding policy, secret owner/audience, requiredness, data-export permission, residency and rebind workflow are not preserved here.

Internal portability types mirror broad database/service DTOs and introduce explicit board_full versus agent_safe modes, while runtime/adapter defaults begin to be encoded in the same module—further evidence that serialization, policy, product UX and vendor runtimes lack separation.

Lines 751-1000 hardcode default runtime and adapter settings for Codex, Gemini, OpenCode, Cursor, Claude and OpenClaw, including Paperclip-specific fixed session/admin scope defaults. Provider configuration migration is therefore coupled to this central service and will drift whenever adapters evolve.

Permission grants accept known keys but silently discard malformed/unknown entries and preserve any plain-record scope without a versioned scope schema or warning. This can quietly reduce or distort authority during migration instead of producing an explicit review plan.

Comment/document/work-product parsers are tolerant: malformed entries are skipped, invalid dates become null, labels and blockers are deduplicated, and arbitrary work-product metadata survives. Warnings are English strings; authorUserId, URLs and metadata lack explicit privacy/egress classification, while documents normalize referenced paths but do not yet prove existence or content binding.

Lines 1001-1250 normalize embedded assets/blobs/attachments but only require nonempty sha256 strings, not canonical 64-hex digests; byte sizes are merely nonnegative/unbounded, content types and filenames are untrusted strings, and attachment comment indices are not checked against the comment collection here.

Import silently injects --skip-git-repo-check into Codex-local adapter arguments. This changes runtime security posture during data migration and is provider-specific behavior that must instead be an explicit, reviewed Connector compatibility decision.

Routine variables/triggers are permissively normalized and imported timer heartbeat is disabled by default—a useful safety instinct. However absolute/system-path detection is heuristic recursive string scanning and executable settings remain interleaved with serialization rather than passed through a versioned capability/policy admission layer.

Lines 1251-1500 translate workspace IDs to portable keys and may execute local git subprocesses against database-supplied cwd values to infer remote/ref/default branch. execFile avoids shell injection, but there is no timeout/path ownership boundary and exported remote URLs are not scrubbed for embedded credentials or restricted schemes.

Workspace deduplication signature uses only name/repoUrl/repoRef/defaultRef, ignoring visibility, source type, setup/cleanup commands and metadata; distinct security/execution configurations can collapse into one exported workspace.

Arbitrary setup/cleanup commands remain portable unless they contain an absolute-path fragment, and arbitrary repository schemes/metadata are retained. The heuristic removes some machine paths but does not constitute executable-code admission or data-egress governance.

Lines 1501-1750 migrate legacy recurrence into enabled cron triggers with validation and explicit errors for unsupported shapes. End bounds (until/count) are deliberately discarded with only a warning, so a previously finite task can become indefinitely recurring.

The cron approximations are not semantically equivalent for interval schedules: hourly start-23/step resets daily and daily */N is day-of-month based rather than elapsed-day cadence. Migrated automations are labeled but enabled in the manifest, making approval/pause policy load-bearing later in import.

Routine trigger kinds/policies and cron syntax are checked here, which is stronger than the earlier permissive normalization, but the migration contract still lacks a machine-readable semantic-loss classification requiring human acceptance before activation.

Lines 1751-2000 provide deterministic collision naming and file/selection helpers, but binary decoding and streamToBuffer have no local decoded-size/aggregate-memory limit; Node base64 decoding is permissive and unsupported encodings alone fail closed.

normalizeFileMap normalizes and root-strips every path into one object but silently overwrites earlier entries when distinct raw paths normalize to the same key. There is no collision error/provenance record at this boundary, enabling ambiguous or attacker-controlled last-write-wins content.

Agent tree sorting treats missing parents as roots but omits pure cycles and uses repeated queue.shift, which is quadratic for large flat organizations. Sidebar selection/YAML filtering is presentation-aware and depends on path-derived slugs rather than a signed entity/file inventory.

Lines 2001-2250 prune labels/assets/blobs/sidebar metadata for selected exports, but filterExportFiles accepts an arbitrary selected path set and does not itself close transitive dependencies. It can retain manifest references whose actual blob/document file was not selected, producing an internally incomplete package unless callers perfectly expand dependencies.

Extension discovery prefers root names but otherwise takes the first nested suffix match. ensureMarkdownPath checks only .md after slash replacement and does not normalize/reject traversal at this point.

Portable adapter config is produced with a field blacklist (cwd, instruction/prompt paths, env, skill sync). Unknown future filesystem, credential or executable fields are exported by default; this repeats the unsafe policy-drift pattern. Default pruning uses JSON serialization equality and may drop explicit false values or map undefined array entries into later nulls, changing configuration intent.

Lines 2251-2500 recursively strip null/empty values, which improves readability but can erase meaningful explicit empty/null reset semantics. The iterative YAML renderer avoids call-stack/argument overflow for large structures, a good robustness detail.

YAML scalar values are JSON quoted, but object keys are emitted raw. Arbitrary metadata/config keys containing YAML delimiters, control characters or newlines are not escaped here, creating parser divergence or document injection risk in the hand-rolled format.

Selected-file import/export rebuilds COMPANY.md includes and always injects the company document even if not selected. It normalizes selected paths but still relies on the normalized map's last-write behavior and rebuilds entity truth from a presentation package rather than verifying a signed file/entity inventory.

Lines 2501-2750 build skill references from the server process cwd git HEAD and mutable master URLs/trackingRef. The commit may be null or unrelated when cwd is not the source checkout, and withSkillSourceMetadata appends another source entry on each pass without deduplication, so exports are not necessarily stable/idempotent.

The custom YAML parser is intentionally a small subset but is highly tolerant: invalid lines/indentation are skipped, duplicate keys overwrite, malformed quoted/JSON values become raw strings, and unquoted colons are structural. No depth/line/key/value/resource caps appear in this parser segment.

Keys are assigned into ordinary objects without a forbidden-key check or null prototype. __proto__/constructor/prototype inputs can alter local object prototypes or interact dangerously with later Object.assign/spread operations; this requires dedicated adversarial testing and a hardened parser/data container.

Lines 2751-3000 fetch remote text/binary/JSON fully into memory and propagate the full URL/status into errors; no local response-size/content-type limit is visible. Env inputs dedupe case-insensitively with first-wins semantics and build ordinary key-indexed objects, repeating reserved-key/prototype hazards.

Import value resolution falls back from scoped agent/project keys to a global key of the same name. A single supplied secret can therefore bind across multiple principals/scopes unless the caller provides every scoped value, with no data-owner/audience confirmation.

readCompanyApprovalDefault unconditionally returns false, so package reconstruction discards any company-level new-Agent approval default instead of preserving or requiring explicit review. This is a direct governance-semantic loss.
Remote/environment parsing remains tolerant and string-driven; source URLs, secret labels/keys and env descriptions are not yet bound to structured provenance, classification or stable error codes.

Lines 3001-3250 reject only schema versions newer than 6 and otherwise parse every positive legacy number without an explicit per-version migration pipeline. Referenced paths are unioned with every discovered AGENTS/PROJECT/TASK/SKILL file, so unreferenced hidden package content is automatically admitted rather than requiring an allowlisted manifest.

Company reconstruction carries feedbackDataSharingEnabled plus prior consent timestamp, user ID and terms version into the manifest. Consent from another deployment/account context is not inherently transferable; Company OS must require re-consent and preserve old consent only as historical evidence.

Agent fields accept explicit unnormalized/duplicate slugs, arbitrary roles/config/permissions/metadata and default missing adapter type to process. Malformed known permission grants are silently dropped. Safety depends on later validation rather than a typed manifest boundary.

Skill parsing scans all file keys for every skill (O(skills×files)) and trusts the first metadata source. Arbitrary source hostname/URL/trackingRef and mutable refs are reconstructed, while commit may be absent; source provenance and later network resolution are not yet constrained to a verified digest.

Lines 3251-3500 admit project/task slugs and most project/workspace/issue execution, adapter override, metadata, billing, monitor and relationship fields as loosely typed records/strings. Status/priority and referential integrity are deferred, while older-schema semantic losses remain only a warning.

GitHub URL parsing enforces HTTPS but accepts any hostname, credentials and query-provided ref/path/companyPath after only slash trimming; dot segments are not rejected here. Tree URLs also treat only one path segment as ref, so branch names containing slashes are ambiguous.

The service composes nearly every domain service plus mutable environment-controlled secret mode. Imported Agent permission application first creates membership then loops individual grants without one transaction; partial authority can persist, and grantedByUserId may be null for Agent-initiated import.

Provider-specific OpenCode validation and adapter registry admission live inside portability. This confirms adapter compatibility must be isolated behind Connector-owned import planners rather than copied into Company OS core.

Lines 3501-3750 materialize supplied secrets one by one before binding them into the manifest, tracking created IDs for later cleanup but without an evident transaction in this segment. Secrets use the configured default provider and latest version, actorUserId may be null, and scoped inputs can still receive a global fallback value.

Remote GitHub resolution falls main→master, suppresses recursive-tree errors into an empty tree, then sequentially fetches every Markdown and every path under skills plus explicit includes. There is no visible file/count/aggregate-byte/concurrency cap; a large or hostile repository can cause many network calls and memory growth.

Include paths are joined to basePath without rejecting dot segments here, and arbitrary HTTPS hostnames are supported. This creates an egress/SSRF and repository-boundary question delegated to ghFetch/URL helpers; Company OS requires an explicit destination allowlist and normalized path containment proof.

The export path begins by loading managed-resource markers, all Agents including terminated, full skills and other domain data into memory. Built-in/terminated resources are filtered with warnings, showing product-specific lifecycle policy embedded in serialization.

Critical lines 3751-4000 implement explicit-selector fallback unsafely: if include.agents/projects/issues is true but every requested selector is missing or skipped, the empty selected map is interpreted as select all. A typo or forbidden built-in selector can therefore export the entire category rather than nothing/error, violating data minimization and user intent.
Issue selector dispatch uses contains('-') to choose identifier lookup; UUID IDs also contain hyphens, so direct UUID selection is misrouted and can trigger the export-all fallback above.

Issue/project selector resolution performs sequential service calls, project-issue expansion can load full lists repeatedly, and routine details use unbounded Promise.all. The whole export is memory-resident with no pagination/snapshot boundary, so data can be inconsistent under concurrent writes and expensive for large companies.

Permission grants and built-in/archived/terminated filtering are copied into export-specific maps with silent drops and warnings rather than governed export policy/evidence. No per-data-domain authorization is visible inside the service.

Critical lines 4001-4250 repeat the selector bug for skills and appear to export selectedSkillRows without an include.skills guard. Because skills are loaded whenever Agents are included (the default), an Agent-only/default export can place every non-managed company skill file into the bundle even when include.skills is false.

Skill file reads are sequential and failures are silently ignored, yielding incomplete packages without a warning. Agent instruction files, arbitrary metadata/config/permissions and project workspace commands are assembled into one in-memory file map; only a single adapter command field gets an absolute-path check.
Company logo storage streams are fully buffered, and raw storage/asset errors are copied into warnings. Exported binary size/content is not bounded here.
Task export begins per-issue comment and relationship service calls inside a loop, creating clear N+1 behavior. Labels are loaded once and missing references warned, which is the stronger pattern.

Lines 4251-4500 add per-task document, work-product and attachment queries/storage reads, compounding N+1 and fully buffering every attachment. Blob bytes are correctly rehashed and deduplicated rather than trusting stale database hashes—a strong integrity pattern—but no total/file size cap or snapshot consistency is visible.

Raw board user IDs on comments are deliberately removed, improving privacy but collapsing author identity to kind=user; arbitrary presentation/metadata still travels. Company OS needs pseudonymous/source principal references and provenance, not either raw cross-tenant IDs or erased accountability.

Invalid comment timestamps can throw during new Date(...).toISOString(), while missing external blocker/workspace/run references are dropped with English warnings. Migration loss is not structured or acceptance-gated.

Embedded asset export correctly verifies asset.companyId before reading bytes, blocking crafted cross-company asset URLs. It still performs sequential asset/storage reads into memory and derives ownership from regex matches in rendered text/JSON rather than an authoritative relation table.

Lines 4501-4750 serialize prior feedback-sharing consent into the bundle, rebuild the parsed manifest twice, and generate an org-chart PNG through a route-layer renderer. Renderer errors are silently swallowed; transport preview invokes the full export including storage, local instructions, Git/GitHub and image rendering instead of a cheap side-effect-free plan.

README and org-chart presentation artifacts are inserted after selection/reparse rules with special cases, while the manifest has no authoritative complete file inventory/digest. Package truth is repeatedly re-derived from files, increasing parser differential and selection inconsistency risk.

Import preview correctly treats missing explicitly selected Agent slugs as errors (unlike export selector fallback), validates referenced Markdown existence and checks ambiguous skill references. However ensureMarkdownPath still only enforces suffix, and warning/error contracts remain localized English strings.
The previewExport issues expression contains Boolean(...) ?? false, whose fallback is unreachable; minor dead logic illustrates how this monolith mixes planning and execution semantics.

Lines 4751-5000 validate routine/workspace references and plan collisions against current target Agents/projects/skills, but the preview is not bound to a target revision/lease; actual state can change before apply, invalidating names and overwrite decisions.

Existing Agent matching is based on normalized display name slug, projects on urlKey, and skills on key OR slug. Replace can therefore update a coincidental target entity rather than a provenance-bound identity; source reportsToExistingAgentId is also trusted if an opaque ID happens to exist in the target.

nameOverrides are applied to issuePlans before issuePlans are populated, so task title overrides are silently ignored. Agent/project overrides are not collision-revalidated after replacement and can create duplicates or alter the preview/apply mapping.

Agent-safe project env validation catches errors into raw message strings. Required human/data-owner confirmation, stable codes and an immutable reviewed plan digest are absent from the preview contract.

Lines 5001-5250 verify every blobs/<suffix> file hash before writes, a strong fail-before-mutation integrity step. The suffix is not proven canonical in earlier parsing, and non-blob files such as company logo/Markdown are not sealed by a complete manifest digest.

Import creates or updates the company—including feedback data-sharing consent—before secret materialization and all other entities. There is no enclosing transaction, so later failure leaves a partial company or already-mutated governance/data-sharing state.

Agent-safe new-company import requires merely one active source user membership then copies all active memberships to the new company. It does not require each human to accept the new organization/responsibility contract, and role/authority transfer is automatic.

Board-full creation falls back to synthetic user board when actorUserId is null. Logo upload→asset row→company link is multi-step and failures become warnings; stored objects/assets can orphan and the old/new logo lifecycle is not atomic with the import.

Lines 5251-5500 upload embedded assets before skills/Agents and continue on per-asset errors, leaving partial assets by design. Later import failure has no shown asset/object compensation, only secret IDs are tracked.

Skills are imported whenever include.agents OR include.skills, confirming that an Agent-only import mutates the target skill catalog even when skills were not requested. Package text files are passed broadly to the skill importer and conflict behavior is only rename/skip in safe mode.

Agent replace/create is a long nontransactional chain: mutate Agent, materialize filesystem instruction bundle, add membership/default and imported grants, then sync secret bindings. Materialization failures are downgraded to warnings, so an idle/updated Agent can exist with empty or stale instructions; later failures leave partial authority/configuration.

Replace updates broad Agent configuration but imported permission grants are additive and existing grants are not cleared here, so replace does not reproduce source authority. New Agents receive tasks:assign by default in addition to imported grants, again changing the source permission model.

Lines 5501-5750 assign reporting links after Agent creation and downgrade assignment failures to warnings; no explicit cycle/responsible-human validation is visible here. Opaque existing-manager IDs/slugs can bind source hierarchy to target principals by coincidence.

Project replace updates the project but then creates every imported workspace without reconciling/removing existing workspaces, so replace is additive and may duplicate executable workspace configurations. Secret sync, workspace creation and policy hydration are separate side effects with no rollback.

Board-full import stores repo URLs plus setup/cleanup commands directly in target workspaces. Safe mode's earlier blacklist helps, but full import has no risk approval, code provenance or activation gate for these executable instructions.

Issue import improves performance by prebuffering typed rows for batched writers and resolves labels once. Legacy raw label IDs survive when coincidentally present in the target, another cross-deployment opaque-ID collision that can silently attach unintended labels.

Lines 5751-6000 create each routine and then its triggers in separate calls. Trigger failure leaves a partial routine; imported schedules/webhooks/API triggers may be enabled immediately unless pauseAutomations or missing-assignee behavior prevents execution, with no per-action human approval.

Comment authorship is rewritten: source user comments become authored by the importing user, missing users/Agents become system. This destroys source responsibility provenance; metadata and createdAt travel without a source principal/evidence envelope.

Issue rows and child rows are buffered with pre-generated IDs, a sound performance/atomic-batch preparation pattern. Documents/work products deliberately clear run/workspace/sourceTrust references and monitors land unarmed, good safety choices but still unstructured semantic loss.

Attachment hashes are rechecked and board size limit enforced, but only after the base64/blob has already been decoded and held in memory. This prevents oversized persistence, not memory-exhaustion during parse/apply.

Lines 6001-6179 flush issues, inbox archives, comments, documents, work products, attachments and blocker relations through separate service/database calls. A later failure leaves earlier categories committed; storage objects were uploaded even earlier. There is no whole-import transaction, durable saga or replayable checkpoint.

Only newly created secret IDs receive best-effort compensation on failure, and cleanup errors are swallowed. Companies, memberships, consent, logos/assets, embedded assets, skills, Agents, permissions, instruction bundles, projects/workspaces, routines/triggers, labels, issues and stored objects are not rolled back or reconciled.

Blocking-cycle filtering is a useful fail-soft integrity step and relation insertion is batched/on-conflict-ignore, but repeated queue.shift can become quadratic. Monitors remain unarmed and imported inbox items are suppressed for a board user, both thoughtful operational safeguards.

The result reports company/Agents/skills/projects/routines/env inputs but not imported issue/document/evidence identities or a canonical request/result digest. Route activity is therefore unable to provide a complete immutable responsibility chain for the actual migrated data.

notes: The schema is a large shared aggregate spanning applications, connections, credentials, grants, installs, OAuth state, catalogs, profiles, gateways, invocation, approval, audit, and runtime concerns; it imports many core-company tables directly and is not a narrow connector-owned store.
The deliberate NO ACTION application foreign key is a strong database-level delete/create race defense and is documented with the exact PostgreSQL locking rationale.
Connection grants use a composite company/connection foreign key plus subject-kind checks and partial unique indexes, providing strong tenant and default-grant invariants.

Connection installs use only a single-column connection foreign key; the separate companyId is not tied to the connection's company by a composite foreign key, so cross-tenant inconsistency is structurally possible if service checks fail.
OAuth states persist the PKCE verifier in plaintext and bind actor/session/subject metadata, but issueId and interactionId have no foreign keys in this schema range.
Catalog risk defaults to read and profile defaults to deny; the combination is safer at the profile layer but still preserves the fail-open classification concern for installed read defaults.

Profile entries and bindings carry companyId without composite foreign keys tying the referenced profile/application/connection/catalog rows to the same company, leaving tenant consistency mostly to services.

Gateway bearer tokens are stored hashed and model finite expiry/override evidence, a reusable credential design, but the default TTL is 90 days and policy correctness depends on later checks and migrations.

Gateway sessions bind agent, run, optional issue/gateway/token metadata and store only token hashes with expiry/revocation, which is a useful runtime-proof model; cross-company consistency of those foreign keys is again not enforced by composite constraints.

Invocation rows capture redacted argument/result summaries, hashes, catalog snapshots, policy evidence, credential/header summaries, run/issue/agent context, and structured error code plus message, making them a strong audit substrate but not a complete Company OS responsibility contract.

Invocation idempotency is unique only when a non-null key is supplied; the schema neither requires keys for mutations nor ties them to connection/tool/agent/run scope, so semantics depend on caller discipline.

Action requests bind a canonical argument hash and optional signed arguments to an invocation and approval, but have no unique one-request-per-invocation constraint, no status check, and no database-enforced company consistency with the invocation/approval/issue.

Connection token issuance records requested and issued scope, responsible user, token hash, outcome, error code and a database-bounded 1-900 second ttlSeconds; the bound applies only to the recorded integer and does not constrain the external token's explicit expiresAt.

Tool and gateway rate-limit tables have useful unique window keys, but this schema alone does not provide an atomic consume invariant; the previously observed count-then-act broker path can still race.

The generic tool-access audit table retains structured reason codes and actor ids but lacks first-class accountable-human, run, issue, approval, evidence, and responsibility-contract links; richer tool_call_events partly duplicate it instead of one canonical responsibility ledger.

The complete schema confirms strong redaction, token-hash, idempotency-option, and audit ideas alongside widespread service-enforced tenant invariants and duplicated operational/audit models; migrations and schema tests remain required before a final database judgment.

notes: The client validates database tuning environment variables and safely quotes dynamic SQL identifiers/literals, supporting both direct and transaction-pooler deployments without embedding vendor-specific behavior in callers.

Manual pending migrations are ordered by the Drizzle journal and each migration plus its history entry executes in one explicit transaction, so ordinary statement failure rolls back that migration atomically.

There is no advisory lock or other cross-process migration lease in this range. Concurrent server startups can both observe a missing history entry and race through DDL/data backfills, especially for non-idempotent later migrations.

History existence is satisfied by hash OR filename when both columns exist. A file changed in place but retaining its name can therefore be treated as already applied, weakening immutable migration integrity in name-aware journals.

Journal creation and migration bookkeeping support several historical table shapes, a pragmatic upgrade feature, but created_at is synthesized from local metadata/current time and is not a cryptographic ordering guarantee.

Statement splitting relies exclusively on the custom breakpoint marker and manual unsafe execution; correctness therefore depends on every migration author placing markers around multi-statement SQL accurately.
The runner contains schema-object introspection helpers used for history repair; the remaining lines must establish whether that repair validates exact definitions or merely object presence.

History repair recognizes only CREATE TABLE, ADD COLUMN, CREATE INDEX, and ADD CONSTRAINT and checks object-name presence, not column types/defaults, index columns/predicates, foreign-key targets/actions, check expressions, or constraint validation state.

If every recognized object exists, reconciliation can insert or update a journal entry for the current file hash even when the installed schema definition differs materially, converting undetected drift into an apparently up-to-date database.

Unrecognized statements fail closed for history repair and processing stops at the first unreconciled migration, a useful ordering safeguard; however, ordinary manual application then executes those statements without a cross-instance lock.

Applied-migration inference has multiple best-effort fallbacks from hashes to timestamps, ids, and finally row counts. This improves legacy recovery but can misclassify history when migration files changed, journal rows are partial, or timestamps differ.
Non-empty databases without any migration journal are correctly rejected rather than auto-initialized, a strong fail-closed bootstrap rule.
There is no down-migration API, snapshot restore hook, migration preflight for destructive/locking operations, compatibility window contract, or deployment-level expand/contract gate in this client.

The database reset helper validates identifiers and terminates connections before drop/recreate, but it is a destructive administrative primitive whose caller authorization and deployment exposure must be audited elsewhere.

The complete runner is pragmatic for small self-hosted installs but its best-effort drift repair, lack of advisory locking, and absence of online/rollback orchestration are not sufficient as-is for Company OS managed-cloud or enterprise upgrade guarantees.

notes: The migration safety checker currently defines only four rule families, all centered on mutation/index behavior for known-large tables; it does not yet claim to cover destructive DDL, tenant/credential semantics, foreign-key locks, NOT NULL rewrites, irreversible changes, or mixed-version compatibility.
Findings use deterministic content-derived ids and a baseline/new/stale model, which is a useful review workflow for introducing safety gates into an existing migration history.
The SQL splitter handles explicit Drizzle breakpoints, quotes, dollar-quoted blocks, nested block comments, and semicolons more carefully than simple regex-only tooling.

Any rule or all rules can be suppressed through an inline comment carrying a nonempty reason; this provides accountable escape hatches only if code review validates the reason, because there is no issue id, approver, expiry, or scope beyond the containing statement.
Index parsing intentionally ignores expression columns when deciding whether a plain-column access path exists, reducing false assurance for batched ORDER BY operations.

The implementation is a targeted large-table performance guard, not a general migration safety system; remaining lines and tests must be checked before judging parser reliability and false-negative surface.
Predicate and index analysis normalizes quoting, aliases, sort modifiers, conjunctive partial-index predicates, and expression columns with considerably more care than a naive grep-based guard.

Mutation discovery targets UPDATE and DELETE only; INSERT...SELECT backfills, ALTER TABLE rewrites, CREATE TABLE AS, TRUNCATE, DROP, type changes, constraint validation and trigger-driven mutations are outside this parser path.

The checker treats the presence of LIMIT/FETCH plus any DML as a batched mutation and detects DO-loop patterns, but correctness depends on later correlation between the limiting subquery, target table, ordering columns and support indexes.

Selective-WHERE recognition is syntactic and accepts a broad family of comparisons, IN, EXISTS, LIKE and null checks; it cannot estimate selectivity or distinguish a predicate matching nearly every row without table statistics.

The parser deliberately tracks parentheses, comments, quotes and qualified references to reduce false positives, but remains a hand-built SQL recognizer whose supported grammar and exclusions must be treated as a bounded lint contract, not semantic proof.

Support indexes are collected from the entire migration before mutations are analyzed, so an index declared after a large-table mutation can suppress a finding even though it did not support that mutation at execution time.

When any explicit table-size estimates are supplied, tables absent from that estimate map are treated as not large instead of falling back to the known-large catalog, allowing partial telemetry input to create false negatives.

The checker recommends CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY for known-large tables, but the already-read manual migration runner wraps every migration in BEGIN/COMMIT. PostgreSQL forbids CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction, creating a direct contradiction between the safety remediation and the production runner.

For batched mutations without ORDER BY, any overlap between a predicate column and any same-migration index column/predicate is accepted; this is weaker than proving the index supports the actual filter and batch progression.
The baseline mechanism fails only on new findings. Stale baseline ids are explicitly ignored, so removed/changed historical statements leave dead suppressions without failing CI.

The command scans every SQL migration and emits stable, reviewable evidence. As a narrow large-table lint it is useful, but it is not a canonical migration safety owner and cannot substantiate claims about upgrade, rollback, data integrity, authorization, or zero-downtime readiness.
The complete implementation merits ADAPT for parser/test patterns only, with the rule model expanded and the transaction/concurrent-index contradiction resolved before Company OS use.

notes: The 6,316-line service is another very broad orchestration boundary spanning gateway authentication, sessions/tokens, rate limits, profiles/policies, approvals, secrets, remote HTTP, local subprocesses, plugins, Paperclip self-tools, audit and UI-facing previews.

Gateway and session tokens use random 256-bit suffixes and are persisted by SHA-256 hash; session TTL and Tool timeouts are bounded, while named gateway tokens may be long-lived according to separately stored policy.

Caller metadata headers are length- and CR/LF-sanitized, sensitive passthrough names are blocked and audited endpoints omit query/fragment, which are useful secret-exposure defenses; endpoint paths can still contain embedded credentials or sensitive ids.
Unknown Tool names default to read risk in inferToolRisk. Catalog flags improve classification, but any missing/misclassified catalog metadata can still fail open at this layer.

The stable serialization/hash helper has no explicit rejection for undefined, bigint, cycles, non-finite numbers or Unicode normalization; exact approval/idempotency binding must therefore be checked against validated inputs and the separately audited content guard.

The prosumer approval preview interpolates argument keys and string values directly into Markdown without escaping. Its identifier filter recognizes separator-delimited id/key/token/hash names but misses camelCase fields such as noteId, so it can leak identifiers and permit Markdown presentation manipulation in a human decision surface.

Built-in fixtures, Paperclip self-tools, local stdio templates, provider-specific Google Sheets environment keys and virtual search/run tools live in the same service, making this unsuitable as a vendor-neutral Company OS core module.

Protocol rate limiting begins with a database upsert design rather than the count-then-act pattern observed in the token broker; the remaining query/result semantics and all execution paths still require review.

Protocol rate-limit consumption is an atomic INSERT...ON CONFLICT count increment, a strong reusable pattern, although expired-counter pruning performs a global delete from a request path and later enforcement/audit ordering still need review.

Connected Tool discovery applies explicit company, status, health, quarantine, transport and application filters. Per-connection discovery nevertheless loads every eligible company Tool and filters in memory, creating unnecessary tenant-scale work.
Plugin Tools receive the same fail-open name heuristic and cannot supply a first-class risk declaration in this path.

Run-context resolution strongly binds company, Agent, active run, snapshot issue/project and referenced tenant objects. It does not bind a versioned accountable human or ResponsibilityContract in this range.

The 'last changed by' access hint can attribute only createdByAgentId on policies/bindings and returns null for human or profile/entry edits. It can therefore present incomplete or misleading provenance on a governance UI.

writeAudit writes tool_access_audit_events and the general activity log sequentially without a transaction/outbox. Failure of the second write returns an error after the dedicated audit is committed; several distinct actions are also collapsed into generic policy_decision/call_failed classifications.

Session validation reads revocation/expiry/run state and then updates lastUsedAt by id only. A concurrent revocation after the read can still yield a usable session for one call because the final update is not a guarded claim.
An invalid token containing a real session UUID triggers a durable auth-failure audit for that session, creating an unauthenticated audit-amplification path unless an outer limiter always intervenes.
Interaction lifecycle reflection is read-modify-write without version/CAS protection and can overwrite concurrent interaction result changes.

Approval setup updates Invocation, ActionRequest, signed arguments, interaction and events through separate writes; the shown missing-context and missing-signing-secret paths already demonstrate partial-state transitions rather than one atomic approval command.

Destructive Tools create a formal approvals row while ordinary writes use only the issue interaction confirmation path; the formal-risk threshold is hard-coded to destructive instead of a company/data/action policy decision.

Formal approval, issue link, interaction, ActionRequest update, ToolCallEvent and two audit streams are sequential independent writes. Any intermediate failure can leave orphan approval/interaction state or a parked invocation without its complete responsibility evidence.

The technical approval Markdown embeds a JSON summary in a code fence and the prosumer preview embeds raw fields; adversarial backticks/Markdown can alter presentation even if the stored canonical hash remains intact.

Tool listing and on-demand search load all connected Tools and perform one asynchronous policy decision per Tool on every request. This is an unbounded N+1-style policy projection with no pagination, cache/version key or database-side filtering.

The Paperclip self get_issue_context Tool checks only Agent session presence and company ownership of the requested issue. It does not require the issue to be the run's issue, assigned to the Agent, or otherwise authorized, so a Tool-enabled Agent can request arbitrary known issue ids within its company.

Remote endpoint parsing and public-network validation are applied before execution, and header precedence correctly lets managed credentials override metadata/static/caller values while dropping reserved and sensitive caller headers.

Static headers are allowed from connection config without the sensitive-header prohibition applied to caller passthrough. Operators can therefore store Authorization/API-key-like values directly in ordinary JSON config and forward them, bypassing the Secret reference/audit boundary.

Optional metadata headers export company, Agent, issue, project, run and session identifiers to the remote provider; this is configurable but not visibly authorized through a Company OS-style data egress contract.
Credential resolution records system access and marks connection health on failure, but connection health writes are separate side effects that can race with concurrent successful calls.

Approval snapshots bind application/connection/catalog identity and status, configuration hashes, credential-reference hashes and exact resolved Secret versions. This is a strong reusable stale-approval defense, though later execution must prove it is compared immediately before dispatch.

Local stdio inherits only a small OS environment allowlist, which limits ambient Secret leakage. Template env values are nevertheless read directly from ordinary connection config rather than Secret references, allowing credentials such as service-account JSON to reside in non-secret configuration.

The local stdio stdout accumulator is unbounded until a newline arrives; a malicious or broken child can exhaust memory. SIGTERM is followed by an unbounded wait for process exit, so a child that ignores the signal can defeat the advertised timeout.

Local JSON-RPC parsing matches numeric ids but does not visibly validate jsonrpc version, response shape or duplicate responses; returned error objects are attached to gateway error details and require downstream redaction review.

Remote HTTP uses manual redirect rejection, AbortController timeout and a 1 MB declared/actual body check. The actual-size check occurs only after response.text() buffers the full body, so an absent/false Content-Length can still cause memory pressure beyond the limit.

Individual call failures and successes update shared connection health through independent last-writer-wins writes; concurrent calls can make health oscillate or allow an older result to overwrite newer state.

Remote elicitation converts provider-controlled messages/schema into human interaction content and stores the requested schema in event metadata. Length/count caps help presentation, but no data-classification or prompt-injection boundary is applied before the external content enters the human/Agent workflow.
Elicitation reuses Invocation status awaiting_approval and policy decision defer_runtime, conflating missing Tool input with governance approval in operational state projections.

The generic runWithTimeout races a timer against a promise but does not cancel the underlying operation. A timed-out builtin/plugin execution can continue and perform a side effect after the caller and audit path record timeout.

Named gateway tokens validate hash, gateway status, revocation, expiry and heartbeat-run company/Agent/active context, then apply atomic token- and gateway-level protocol limits. This is a strong layered bearer boundary.

Token lastUsedAt is updated before protocol rate limiting and without a guarded revoked/expiry predicate. A concurrent revocation can still permit one request, and throttled requests appear as successful token use.

Non-run named gateway sessions are attributed as system even when the gateway is Agent-scoped; there is no accountable-human subject or current membership/responsibility validation in the session identity.

Null-expiry named tokens are projected with a synthetic expiry ten years in the future, underscoring that long-lived bearer credentials are a supported operating mode rather than an exceptional short-lived runtime proof.
Authentication failures are durably audited only after the failure limiter is exceeded; lower-volume invalid/revoked/expired attempts leave no audit event in this function.

Test Tool execution marks the invocation executing and writes an allow audit before dispatch, then performs the external side effect before success event/audit persistence. Any later validation or database/audit failure can report failure after the side effect occurred, and retry can duplicate it.
The execution catch returns decision=allowed even with an error object, conflating authorization decision with execution outcome in the API contract.

Critical correctness bug: runApprovedTestInvocation always reflects the interaction lifecycle as executed after awaiting runTestToolInvocation, but runTestToolInvocation catches execution failures and returns an error instead of throwing. Approved test calls that fail can therefore be shown as executed in the human interaction while the Invocation is failed/timed_out.

Result prompt-injection validation happens after the external action. Blocking a malicious result protects downstream context but cannot undo the side effect; the audit must distinguish executed-with-quarantined-result from execution failure.
The gateway still lacks an atomic execution claim/outbox or provider idempotency proof that closes the side-effect/persistence gap.

Approved Agent actions use an atomic approved-to-executing claim and wait/replay behavior, verify signed canonical arguments, compare live remote target/Secret-version snapshots and check issue openness twice before dispatch. These are strong single-execution and stale-target patterns.

The execution helper contains a stuck-state branch: after winning the executing claim, a legacy signed payload with executionOnApprove not true throws without a terminal update. Current public callers guard executionOnApprove before invoking the helper and the linked regression test keeps legacy requests approved, so this appears defensive/unreachable in audited paths rather than a demonstrated production bug; any new caller could expose it.
Issue-closed expiry updates the ActionRequest and interaction but not the Invocation approval/status, leaving split lifecycle state.

Approval execution does not re-evaluate current Tool policy, Profile binding, Agent authority, accountable human or ResponsibilityContract. The signed snapshot excludes those governance versions, so permission/policy revocation after approval does not prevent dispatch.

Execution events are attributed to the original Agent session, not the approving human, and the approver identity is not carried into the call event shown here. This breaks the direct human-decision-to-side-effect responsibility link.
Success/failure persistence across Invocation, ActionRequest, interaction and ToolCallEvent remains nontransactional after the external side effect.

Matching/replay keys use company, issue, Agent, Tool name and argument hash but omit run, connection/catalog identity, policy/contract version and explicit idempotency key. A prior approved/executed request can be reused across a later run on the same issue; only remote Tools receive the snapshot defense.
Approved requests are not rejected when their expiresAt has passed; expiry handling applies only while status is pending.

Named gateway creation, Profile binding and audit are separate writes. Updating a gateway to a new Profile inserts the new binding but never removes the old gateway/Profile binding, potentially retaining or combining stale authority.

Named bearer token create/revoke methods shown here have no audit write and revoke accepts no actor, despite changing persistent execution authority. Null expiry is accepted at service level and raw token is returned once.

Ephemeral session creation inserts the bearer authority and writes its audit record as separate operations. An audit failure can return an error after leaving a live session token persisted, while the caller may not retain the returned token needed to revoke it.

Discovery audit records the complete list of visible Tool names on every listing. This aids traceability but creates potentially large and sensitive audit payloads without an evident cap or classification step.

listPluginToolsForAgent filters through policy but strips providerType and risk from the returned descriptors. Downstream consumers therefore cannot independently display or validate the exact risk classification used by the decision engine.
The management test-call path generates a fresh random idempotency key for every request, so a client retry cannot identify or safely deduplicate the same intended external side effect.

Test-call argument inspection runs in redact/ignore mode and uses the resulting summary for human approval, while policy and execution still receive the original parameters. This avoids automatic prompt-injection blocking but makes the quality of the redacted approval representation critical.

Approval requests produced by test calls receive signed canonical arguments and a one-hour expiry, but creation still spans policy invocation/action rows, snapshot/secret resolution, ActionRequest update, event and audit writes without a transaction or compensating state machine.

getTestCallStatus correctly constrains ActionRequest, Invocation, company, connection and test-origin marker before returning status, preventing it from becoming an arbitrary cross-connection request oracle.

approveActionRequest accepts both pending and already-approved states before the remaining resume logic. The subsequent range must confirm expiry enforcement, atomic claim behavior, actor authorization and idempotent replay for this public approval entry point.

The direct approveActionRequest path validates the signature and optional formal-approval status, then atomically changes pending to approved. It does not check ActionRequest.expiresAt before approval, so an expired request can be approved and, for test calls or executionOnApprove Agent calls, dispatched immediately.

The approval service records either an Agent id or user id supplied by its caller but performs no actor membership, role, separation-of-duties or accountable-human authorization check itself. Correctness is therefore dependent on every route/caller enforcing the right decision authority.

If a request is already approved, approveActionRequest can trigger executeApprovedAgentInvocation again; the inner approved-to-executing claim limits duplicate dispatch, but approval and execution remain coupled to a read-time branch rather than an explicit durable command/outbox.

declineActionRequest atomically rejects a pending request and updates Invocation.approvalState, but this range emits no ToolCallEvent/audit and does not reflect the rejection onto the linked interaction, yielding an incomplete human-decision evidence chain compared with approval.

Virtual search_tools bypasses the ordinary policy service and records a hard-coded allow decision. It may only expose already-filtered discovery, but its authority and data-return policy are encoded in bespoke control flow rather than the canonical policy boundary.

The main executeTool resume path strongly scopes an approved request to company, current issue, Agent, run, originating requester, linked interaction and exact Tool, and unlike the direct approval path explicitly expires both pending and approved requests before use.

An accepted issue interaction can promote a pending ActionRequest to approved and copy resolver identity into the decision record. This service does not independently verify that the resolver is an authorized human for the exact risk/action/data scope.

Expiry and interaction-driven approval update ActionRequest/interactions/events through separate writes and still do not consistently synchronize Invocation approval/status, leaving recoverable but real projection divergence risks.

The explicit resume route revalidates signed arguments and the live remote approval snapshot, then atomically consumes approved to executed before dispatch. The label executed therefore means execution claimed, not side effect completed, and a process crash can strand the request while preventing retry.

Consuming an approval writes resolvedByAgentId to the executing session Agent even though the row already carries the human/Agent decision fields. This mixes executor and resolver semantics on the same record and complicates direct responsibility projection.

A fresh call flows through the policy service, durable Invocation/idempotency recording and an explicit require-approval branch. Policy idempotent replay returns only the stored resultSummary rather than the original result, so replay response semantics differ from first execution unless callers expect a summary projection.

After a request is approved, the execution path does not call the policy service again; signature and remote-target freshness are enforced, but revoked Profile/policy/Agent/data authority remains outside the resume invariant.

Result content validation occurs after dispatch and a blocked result is persisted as a failed Invocation with a deny policyDecision in the event/audit. This protects consumers but semantically mislabels an executed external side effect as denied/failed, which can trigger unsafe retries.

Invocation, interaction, ToolCallEvent and dual audits are updated sequentially on both success and failure. A crash after the provider action or any persistence failure leaves no atomic evidence that distinguishes not-run, ran-with-missing-record and safely retryable states.

Runtime capacity and timeout failures are grouped as deferred, but the timeout wrapper cannot prove cancellation for plugin/builtin work. A deferred classification can therefore coexist with a still-running side effect.
Stable structured reason codes are consistently emitted alongside English messages in these paths, an API practice Company OS can adopt without coupling functionality to UI language.

The direct plugin route validates Agent actors against company/Agent/run and resolves the run context, but no equivalent user-actor authorization is visible inside the service. Human access control must be guaranteed entirely by the calling route.

Plugin execution repeats the policy/invocation/audit pipeline and supports approval creation, but unlike the main gateway path it calls pluginToolDispatcher.executeTool without runWithTimeout. A hung plugin can hold the request indefinitely despite Tool timeout conventions elsewhere.

The plugin path has the same side-effect-before-validation/evidence gap and the same semantic error of recording blocked post-execution content as a denied/failed call. It also returns resultSummary on idempotent replay rather than the original typed result.

Session revocation is company-scoped and can additionally enforce Agent/run scope; it records actor metadata when supplied. The actor is optional and the service does not itself authorize a human revoker, so provenance and authority depend on caller discipline.

Expired sessions are hard-deleted in bulk with no cleanup audit or retained tombstone in this service. Even if Invocation events remain, deleting execution-authority records can weaken forensic reconstruction unless retention is owned elsewhere.

Runtime slot list/stop/restart are exposed through the gateway service and delegate scoping to the supervisor. This further confirms that the service combines product policy, external execution, operational control and administrative lifecycle in one ownership boundary.

Across the full source, the best reusable ideas are hashed bearer tokens, tenant/run binding, atomic rate/claim updates, signed canonical arguments, live Secret/target snapshot comparison, structured reason codes and content summaries. Company OS should not copy this monolith or its Paperclip-specific types and self-tools.

The dominant Company OS gaps are accountable-human and ResponsibilityContract binding, data-egress authorization, transactional evidence/outbox semantics, provider idempotency/cancellation proofs, uniform expiry/revocation checks and separation of approval decision from execution state.

Restart counters, backoff and storm windows live in mutable JSON metadata and are computed by read-modify-write without CAS, allowing concurrent restarts to lose increments or bypass suppression.

Runtime state changes, dedicated audit and general activity are sequential writes without a transaction/outbox. A slot can start or stop while its evidence write fails, and retries may duplicate transitions.
Audit actors are either the Agent or generic system; no accountable human, execution-node identity/attestation or ResponsibilityContract is bound to runtime authority and lifecycle events.

getOrCreateSlot performs select-then-insert without conflict recovery. Even if the database uniquely constrains company/slotKey, concurrent creation can return an avoidable error rather than re-read the winner; capacity is still not reserved atomically.

Caller-provided metadata is spread after fixture, hostId, counters and logs during slot creation, so callers can override supervisor-owned host/accounting fields. A forged hostId can make activeRows undercount host capacity until a later lifecycle write repairs metadata.

ensureRunningSlot does not acquire an exclusive lease. Multiple calls can concurrently mark and use the same connection slot, execute callbacks against the same conceptual stdio process and overwrite metadata/idle state; no queue, fencing token or lease owner protects protocol serialization.

Stuck recovery and explicit stop/restart update by id only after a stale read. They can mark an actively used slot failed/stopped or restart it while another call is executing. startSlot itself does not reserve capacity, and explicit restart bypasses a fresh capacity check.

useFixtureSlot has a different failure path from useConnectionSlot: it marks failure but emits no runtime_failed audit, producing inconsistent evidence for the bundled fixture path.

listSlots remains unpaginated and cleanup-coupled. It returns only active states, hiding failed/stopped operational history from this projection even though rows remain stored.

The acceptance suite covers sequential lazy reuse, idle expiry, capacity, public-host gating, restart suppression and stuck recovery, but not any of these multi-instance races, metadata ownership, real process enforcement or error-Secret leakage.

notes: This is the real out-of-process plugin boundary: one long-lived Node child per installed plugin, shared across its configured companies, with bidirectional JSON-RPC, host callbacks, crash recovery and optional streamed execution logs.

Explicit RPC timeouts bypass the ordinary 15-minute cap and may reach Node's roughly 24.8-day timer maximum. The code assumes callers provide independent inactivity/safety guards; this boundary itself cannot guarantee a bounded call or cancellation for multi-hour executions.

Incoming line and per-execution log defaults are each 128 MiB, far above a conservative control-plane message budget. More importantly, readline must accumulate a line before handleLine can reject its length, so the documented pre-parse bound does not prevent memory growth from a worker that never emits a newline.

A single plugin worker multiplexes companies. The presence of crossCompanyBlocked log routing acknowledges that overlapping cross-company executions share one pipe and cannot safely attribute streaming output; dropping later logs avoids misdelivery but does not isolate plugin memory/state or other host calls.

The host mints invocation ids and stores exact scope/trace parent/log routes rather than trusting worker-supplied company ids, a strong capability-routing pattern that should be traced through message handling before final judgment.

Proactive calls receive a pre-seeded set of company scopes outside any host-issued invocation. This fixes setup-time workflows but creates durable ambient multi-company authority at worker level, without a task, accountable human, purpose/data contract or per-call capability shown here.
WorkerStartOptions accepts resolved config, arbitrary environment variables and execArgv; the remaining spawn path must prove allowlisting, Secret isolation and prohibition of dangerous Node flags.

Crash/backoff state is process-local and no durable worker generation/attestation is present in these definitions. A host restart resets counters and cannot by itself prove which worker generation produced an effect.
The comments promise process isolation, but a Node child alone is not a sandbox: filesystem, network, host credentials and OS resources depend on the later spawn configuration and deployment wrapper.

Host-issued invocation scope is checked for worker-to-host requests, and proactive resolution only admits an explicitly referenced company in a configured set. This is a useful narrow capability pattern, though the proactive set remains ambient multi-company authority.

Critical stream authorization gap: a stream notification without an invocation id, with no matching proactive scope, returns an empty context when no other invocation is active. The stream handler rejects only invalidInvocationScope or an explicit scope mismatch, so an idle worker can send streams.open/emit/close for an arbitrary companyId and reach onStreamNotification.

Open stream channels are keyed only by channel, not company/generation. Same-name channels across companies overwrite each other, and crash cleanup can synthesize a close using worker-supplied company attribution.

Cross-company execute-log routing deliberately fails closed once overlapping companies exist, but it uses a global latch that permanently drops live logs for every affected route. It protects delivery integrity at the cost of incomplete evidence and confirms the shared-worker isolation limitation.

Plugin log notifications spread arbitrary worker-controlled metadata and message into the host logger with no field allowlist, size bound below the very large line cap, Secret redaction or prompt/data classification. A plugin can inject sensitive values and high-cardinality fields into production logs.

Parse errors log the first 200 raw characters of an untrusted worker line, and stderr is logged verbatim plus retained in failure messages. Both paths can persist Secrets or customer data emitted by a plugin.

Host-handler exception messages are logged and returned verbatim to the worker, potentially disclosing internal identifiers, database/provider details or Secret-bearing error text across the trust boundary.

The child environment avoids wholesale process.env inheritance and overwrites key host-controlled fields after options.env, which is good. It still exposes host PATH/NODE_PATH and accepts arbitrary execArgv, with no local enforcement of an allowlist, working directory, uid/gid, filesystem/network isolation or OS resource limits.

Node fork also opens an IPC channel in addition to the documented stdio JSON-RPC path; no message handler is shown here, but the extra channel expands the process interface without an expressed protocol need.

Crash tracking and restart state are memory-only. Pending calls receive worker-unavailable responses, but no durable execution receipt distinguishes a request that was processed before the crash from one never processed, so automatic caller retry can duplicate plugin effects.

Critical crash-loop defect: consecutiveCrashes is reset to zero immediately after every successful initialize. A worker that initializes successfully then crashes seconds later always restarts with count one, so exponential backoff and the ten-consecutive-crash cutoff never escalate for the common post-start crash loop.

RPC timeout only rejects the host promise and removes invocation/log routes; it sends no cancellation to the worker. A timed-out execute can continue mutating external systems, and a caller retry can duplicate the side effect.

The shutdown sequence races shutdown response against exit, but if the worker responds before exiting it waits only an additional 500ms before SIGTERM, not the documented ten-second drain. A cooperative worker acknowledging shutdown before finishing cleanup can be killed prematurely.

Initialization failure kills the child, marks the handle crashed and leaves it in the manager map. Auto-restart is suppressed by intentionalStop, while a later startWorker rejects any existing non-stopped handle; recovery requires an explicit stop/remove path rather than a normal retry.

startInternal sends full manifest, resolved config and database namespace to the child. The manager provides no field-level Secret minimization, per-company config partition or proof that a shared worker cannot retain one tenant's config/data for another tenant's invocation.

Manager startup locking prevents duplicate in-process spawns for one plugin, but it is memory-local and does not coordinate multiple server processes/hosts. There is no durable worker lease, generation or owner fencing.

stopWorker/stopAll can race an in-flight startup and do not coordinate through startupLocks; initialization and stop may interleave, producing rejected startup promises or stale lifecycle notifications.
supportedMethods reported by initialize are stored for diagnostics but not enforced before calls, so capability/version mismatch is discovered only through worker response.

Worker error/stderr messages are embedded in host-thrown errors and manager logs without Secret redaction. Together with earlier raw plugin log paths, the worker boundary is not safe for production credentials or customer content.

The strongest reusable pattern is the host-minted invocation capability with company scope and timeout cleanup. Company OS still needs per-installation/per-company isolation, short-lived runtime attestation, cancellation/idempotency/effect receipts, durable leases and a Secret-safe structured protocol.

Tool and route errors remain mostly free-form English strings with message-substring classification; only ToolGateway errors expose a reasonCode, so clients lack a uniform stable failure contract.

Lines 1401-1700 duplicate bridge and URL-keyed endpoints. Read calls require board access while action calls begin with generic authentication and defer company authorization to an optional body companyId; absent companyId permits an instance-admin global scope, creating an implicit dual-scope contract rather than manifest-declared scope.

Lines 1701-2000 show the SSE bridge correctly requires board and company access and keys subscriptions by plugin/channel/company, but does not verify ready status or a stream capability and has no replay cursor, heartbeat or bounded backpressure contract.

Scoped APIs require ready/running status, manifest capability and declared route, resolve and authorize company scope, restrict JSON bodies to 1 MB, sanitize forwarded request headers and allowlist response headers. These are strong reusable boundary primitives.

Scoped API response bodies are not size-limited, worker status/body schemas are trusted, errors expose raw messages, and checkout enforcement still permits peer Agents for the protected route class; mutation idempotency, timeout/cancel and proof of run ownership are absent.

Lines 2001-2300 keep enable, disable, uninstall and upgrade behind instance-admin checks and emit audit/live events, but lifecycle errors and plugin lastError/log rows are returned verbatim to board users, so Secret and external-system redaction depends entirely on upstream writers.

Health is a shallow registry/manifest/status/lastError projection rather than an active worker, dependency or company-configuration probe. Log queries are bounded to 500 but accept arbitrary level strings and have no cursor pagination.

Configuration reads are company-scoped, while writes are restricted to instance admins even though records are company-owned; this creates an operational bottleneck and does not model delegated company administrators.

Lines 2301-2600 validate configuration against manifest schema, strip the SSRF-capable devUiUrl for non-admins, bind Secret references to the company and synchronize reference metadata without returning Secret values—useful patterns for Company OS.

Secret-reference synchronization occurs before config persistence without an explicit transaction, so a later upsert failure can leave reference metadata inconsistent. Worker notification failures are intentionally swallowed after persistence, yielding eventual configuration activation without a durable delivery/outbox status.

Configuration testing is available to board users and forwards the candidate config to the plugin worker; worker warnings/errors become display strings, and neither this route nor the schema establishes purpose-limited Secret access or accountable-human approval.

Lines 2601-2900 restrict manual job triggering to instance admins and bind job IDs to plugin IDs, but expose raw scheduler errors and provide no request idempotency or accountable approval for side-effecting jobs.

The public webhook route verifies only plugin readiness, declared capability and endpoint key; signature verification is delegated to plugin code after the host has persisted the full parsed payload and every request header, including potentially authorization, cookie and signature material.

Webhook delivery has no host-level tenant resolution, replay/idempotency key, rate limit, retention/redaction, retry/dead-letter or pre-persistence authenticity gate in this route. Invalid unauthenticated traffic can therefore create stored delivery rows and reach the worker.

Company-scoped local-folder inspection is exposed to any board member with company access; validation accepts an arbitrary absolute path and can act as a host-filesystem existence/shape oracle unless lower services impose additional roots not visible here.

Lines 2901-3140 also let any company board member persist an arbitrary validated host path as plugin settings; there is no instance-admin gate, approved root policy, human approval or explicit read-versus-write grant in this route.

The dashboard aggregates process IDs, crash state, raw job errors and global webhook delivery errors for any board user. Because webhook deliveries have no companyId, this projection cannot enforce tenant isolation and can expose cross-company operational metadata.

Overall route verdict: REJECT as a reusable module because of its multi-responsibility surface and inconsistent authority, tenant, evidence and error contracts; ADAPT only narrow primitives such as path canonicalization, scoped company binding, request/response header allowlists, body limits and categorical RPC errors.

Reset deletes the canonical row with no expected revision and returns revision 0. This creates ABA semantics: a client holding expectedRevision=0 from before a create/reset cycle can write as if no intervening policy existed.

Reset erases the actual rules and activity stores only revision/default/count summaries, so historical authorization decisions cannot be reconstructed or cryptographically bound. Caller-supplied activity identity is not verified at the service boundary.
Evaluation has no decision logging/cache/version lease; a skill operation can be authorized at revision N and execute after policy N+1 without binding the action digest to the evaluated revision.
